analysis.one_liner: Cuts copyright protection to 28 years, renewable once, applied retroactively to the largest entertainment companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first day: introduced with zero cosponsors, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, most new works are protected by copyright for the author's life plus 70 years. This bill would cut that to 28 years, with one 28-year renewal available if the holder applies for it. Uniquely, the shortened term would also apply retroactively — but only to copyrights owned by motion-picture or arts-and-entertainment companies worth more than $150 billion, a threshold aimed at a tiny handful of media giants. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and received no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the public would gain: books, films, music, and characters would enter the public domain — free for anyone to republish, adapt, or build on — after 28 or 56 years instead of roughly a century for new works. Smaller creators, libraries, educators, and independent producers would get a much larger pool of free material, and the largest entertainment conglomerates would see decades of remaining exclusive rights on their existing catalogs end on a set schedule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, libraries, and small creators

how_it_helps.text: Copyright would last 28 years from the date the work was secured, renewable once for another 28 years if the holder applies during the final year — instead of the current life-of-the-author-plus-70-years rule for new works.

The shortened term would apply retroactively to copyrights owned by companies with market capitalizations above $150 billion that are in the motion picture or arts and entertainment industries, ending their exclusive control of existing works decades early.
Companies already licensing works from those affected giants would keep their license rights for a limited transition period — up to 10 years — so ongoing uses would not end abruptly.

analysis.who_pays: The largest entertainment and media conglomerates would lose the longest and most valuable part of their existing copyrights, which for major studios are often the most profitable assets. Individual authors and smaller creators would also give up something: new works they create would be protected for at most 56 years rather than for their lifetimes plus 70, meaning their works could legally be copied and sold by others while they are still alive.

drawbacks.text: The flat 28-year term would apply to new works by everyone, not just large companies — so a novelist or songwriter would lose exclusive rights to their own work after at most 56 years, well within their lifetime, instead of the current life-plus-70 rule.

A shorter term reduces the long-run value of creative work, which critics of term cuts argue weakens the incentive to invest in books, films, and music, particularly projects whose value builds slowly.

The retroactive provision does not apply evenly: it targets only companies above a $150 billion market cap in specific entertainment industry codes, making the rule a tailored measure aimed at a few firms rather than a general copyright policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted enormous amounts of creative material into the public domain quickly, which benefits readers, viewers, teachers, and independent creators at the direct expense of the largest studios. The main costs are real: individual creators would see their own lifetime protections cut sharply, and the retroactive clause is drafted so narrowly around a market-cap threshold that it reads as a rule written for one industry segment — or effectively one company — rather than a principled reform of copyright terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Steube introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest entertainment conglomerates are better off: their long existing copyrights on valuable catalogs remain intact, and nothing moved toward a shorter public-domain timetable. Authors and publishers of new works also keep the current life-plus-70-year rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large copyright holders and major studios

for.name: Rep. Greg Steube
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote — for the full two years the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote or a visible coalition: a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no floor or committee action, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Major motion picture and entertainment conglomerates (over $150B market cap)
industries.note: The bill's retroactive clause would cut short decades of remaining exclusive rights on their existing film, TV, and character copyrights, moving hugely valuable catalogs toward the public domain. Their interest in keeping those long monopolies runs directly against the public's access to the works.

industries.industry: Authors, songwriters, and small creative businesses
industries.note: New works they create would be protected for a maximum of 56 years instead of life plus 70, ending their exclusive control during their own lifetimes. Their loss, however, is the public's gain in public-domain material.

A much faster flow of works into the public domain would let them copy, adapt, and distribute material freely. The same works they gain access to are the revenue of the large studios, so this interest is directly opposed to theirs.
